questions.question: Which of the following Governor Generals, under the British rule in India, professionalised, bureaucratised and Europeanised the administration of East India Company?
questions.solution:
Lord Cornwallis (1786–1793) is known as the 'Father of Civil Services in India'. Key contributions:
  • Professionalised and Europeanised the EIC administration.
  • Introduced the Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793).
  • Established the Cornwallis Code, separating revenue from judicial administration.

questions.question: During the British rule in India, which of the following Governor Generals devised the ‘Doctrine of Lapse’, a policy of annexation?
questions.solution:
Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856) devised the Doctrine of Lapse, where a princely state under EIC influence would be annexed if the ruler died without a natural heir. States annexed:
  • Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Jhansi (1854), and Awadh (1856 - on grounds of misgovernance).
  • He is also known for introducing the Railways (1853) and the Telegraph in India.

questions.question: Tansen, the famous musician, often sang in the court of which ruler?
questions.solution:
Tansen (Ramtanu Pandey) was one of the Navaratnas (nine gems) in the court of Mughal Emperor Akbar. Important facts:
  • He was a disciple of Swami Haridas.
  • Famous for compositions like Mian Ki Malhar and Mian Ki Todi.
  • Instrument: He is associated with the Rudra Veena.

questions.question: Which ruler of the Chahamana dynasty made Ajmer his capital?
questions.solution:
Ajayaraja II (1110–1135 CE) was a ruler of the Chahamana (Chauhan) dynasty who founded the city of Ajayameru (modern-day Ajmer) and made it his capital. Additional Info:
  • He defeated the Paramaras of Malwa.
  • His son Arnoraja later expanded the kingdom.

questions.question: Who among the following was the last Mauryan ruler and was killed by his commander-in-chief?
questions.solution:
Brihadratha was the last ruler of the Mauryan Dynasty (c. 187–180 BCE). Historical Context:
  • He was assassinated by his commander-in-chief, Pushyamitra Shunga, during a military review.
  • This event led to the establishment of the Shunga Dynasty.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Indo Greeks.
1. The most celebrated Indo-Greek ruler was Menander.
2. Menander has been identified with King Milinda mentioned in the famous Buddhist text Milindapanho.
3. Milindapanho contains philosophical questions that Milinda asked Amrapali.
4. Impressed by the answers, King Milinda accepted Buddhism as his religion.
Which among the above statements are correct.
questions.solution:
The Indo-Greeks were the first to issue gold coins in India. Points regarding Menander:
  • Menander I (Milinda) was the most famous ruler.
  • He engaged in a philosophical dialogue with Buddhist monk Nagasena.
  • This dialogue is recorded in the text Milindapanho ('Questions of Milinda').
  • Statement 3 is incorrect because he spoke with Nagasena, not Amrapali.

questions.question: Under the Regulating Act of 1773, the King-in-Council created a Supreme Court in which of the following places?
questions.solution:
The Regulating Act of 1773 provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta (Fort William). Details:
  • It was established in 1774.
  • Sir Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice.
  • The Act was the first step by the British Parliament to control and regulate the EIC.

questions.question: Which of the following Acts, enacted by the British Parliament, provided for the establishment of a Law Commission for the consolidation and codification of Indian Laws?
questions.solution:
The Charter Act of 1833 provided for the establishment of a Law Commission to codify Indian laws. Exam Points:
  • Lord Macaulay was appointed as the first Law Member.
  • This Act designated the Governor-General of Bengal as the Governor-General of India.
  • Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor-General of India.

questions.question: Who among the following Mauryan kings turned to Buddhism and its tenet of non-violence after the Kalinga war?
questions.solution:
Ashoka the Great (Mauryan Dynasty) embraced Buddhism after the horrific Kalinga War (261 BCE). Impact:
  • He replaced Bheri Ghosha (war drum) with Dhamma Ghosha (sound of righteousness).
  • He sent missionaries (including son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitra) to Sri Lanka to spread Buddhism.

questions.question: Prithviraj Raso, an epic poem about the life of the 12th century Indian king, Prithviraj Chauhan, was written by:
questions.solution:
Prithviraj Raso is an epic poem composed by Chand Bardai, the court poet of Prithviraj Chauhan. Significance:
  • It narrates the life and valor of the 12th-century king.
  • It details his conflict with Muhammad Ghori and his romance with Sanyogita.

questions.question: The Vijayanagar kingdom was established by ________ in 1336.
questions.solution:
The Vijayanagar Empire was founded by two brothers, Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, in 1336 on the banks of the Tungabhadra River. Dynasties:
  • The empire had four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, and Aravidu.
  • Their capital was Hampi.

questions.question: Which of the following did NOT emerge as a result of disintegration of the Bahmani kingdom during the 16th century?
questions.solution:
The Bahmani Kingdom (founded 1347) disintegrated into five independent sultanates collectively called the Deccan Sultanates. The five were:
  • Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), and Bidar (Barid Shahi).
  • Gaur was located in Bengal, not part of the Deccan sultanates.

questions.question: Who among the following Mauryan king fasted to death and died at Shravanabelagola?
questions.solution:
Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Mauryan Empire, abdicated the throne and became a Jain monk under Bhadrabahu. Death:
  • He performed Sallekhana (fasting unto death) at Shravanabelagola (Karnataka).
  • This site remains a major Jain pilgrimage center.

questions.question: The Arms Act was passed in _____ that prevented Indians from keeping arms without an appropriate license.
questions.solution:
The Indian Arms Act (1878) was passed during the viceroyalty of Lord Lytton. Impact:
  • It made it a criminal offense for Indians to carry arms without a license.
  • This restriction did not apply to Europeans.
  • Passed alongside the Vernacular Press Act (1878) to suppress Indian dissent.

questions.question: Shore temple of Mamallapuram was built by:
questions.solution:
The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) was built by the Pallava Dynasty under Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha). Architecture:
  • It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
  • Represents the transition from rock-cut architecture to structural stone temples.

questions.question: Siddheshvara Mahadeva temple in Bengal depicts the architecture of which dynasty?
questions.solution:
The Siddheshvara Mahadeva temple at Barakar (West Bengal) is a notable example of the Pala Dynasty's architecture. Features:
  • Pala rulers were great patrons of Mahayana Buddhism and art.
  • They also founded the Vikramshila University.

questions.question: Malavikagnimitra, a drama of the 5th century CE, was written by _________.
questions.solution:
Malavikagnimitra is a Sanskrit play written by Kalidasa. Plot:
  • It tells the love story of Agnimitra (Shunga Emperor) and Malavika.
  • Kalidasa's other works include Abhijñānaśākuntalam and Meghadūta.

questions.question: Ravana Phadi cave and Durga Temple at Aihole portray the architectural style of which dynasty?
questions.solution:
The Ravana Phadi cave and Durga Temple at Aihole were built under the Badami Chalukya dynasty. Details:
  • Aihole is often called the 'Cradle of Indian Temple Architecture'.
  • The Durga temple is famous for its unique apsidal (semi-circular) shape.

questions.question: The star-shaped temples were built during the reign of:
questions.solution:
Star-shaped (Stellate) temples were a hallmark of the Hoysala Dynasty architecture. Notable Temples:
  • Chennakeshava Temple (Belur), Hoysaleswara Temple (Halebidu), and Keshava Temple (Somnathpur).
  • They used Soapstone (Chloritic Schist) for intricate carvings.

questions.question: Who among the following was the first president of IOC?
questions.solution:
Demetrius Vikelas was a Greek businessman and writer who served as the first President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) from 1894 to 1896. Note:
  • Pierre de Coubertin was the founder but the second president.

questions.question: Which Rajput princess belonged to the Bhakti tradition of Medieval India, whose songs were devoted to Lord Krishna?
questions.solution:
Mirabai (c. 1498–c. 1546) was a Rajput princess of Mewar and a prominent Bhakti saint. Devotion:
  • She was a devout follower of Lord Krishna.
  • She composed numerous Bhajans in Braj Bhasha and Rajasthani.

questions.question: Which of the following indicates the system introduced by Lord Cornwallis granting legal ownership of land to the zamindars in Bengal in order to get a fixed revenue by a fixed date?
questions.solution:
The Permanent Settlement (1793), introduced by Lord Cornwallis, gave Zamindars hereditary rights to land as long as they paid a fixed revenue to the British. Key points:
  • Revenue was fixed permanently.
  • Introduced the 'Sunset Law' (failure to pay by sunset on a fixed date led to auction of land).

questions.question: Ashtadhyayi, is a Sanskrit treatise on grammar, written in the 6th to 5th century BCE by _________.
questions.solution:
Ashtadhyayi is an ancient Sanskrit treatise on grammar written by Panini. Importance:
  • It defines the standards for Classical Sanskrit.
  • Consists of 8 chapters and roughly 4,000 sutras.

questions.question: Which of the following was established by Jyotirao Govindrao Phule in 1873 to fight against idolatry and caste system?
questions.option_4: Shree Narayan Guru Dharma Paripalana (SNDP) Movement
questions.solution:
The Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth Seekers' Society) was founded by Jyotirao Phule in Pune, Maharashtra, in 1873. Objectives:
  • Aimed at liberating Shudras and Dalits from exploitation by upper castes.
  • Phule also wrote the famous book 'Gulamgiri'.

questions.question: The ‘Tripartite struggle’ was between Gurjara Pratiharas in North India, Palas in Eastern India and ________ in South India.
questions.solution:
The Tripartite Struggle for the control of Kannauj (a symbol of sovereignty) lasted for two centuries between:
  • The Gurjara-Pratiharas (North).
  • The Palas (East).
  • The Rashtrakutas (South).
